steps.title: Rate of reaction
steps.body: How fast a chemical reaction takes place. It measures how quickly reactants are used up or how quickly products are formed.

steps.title: Collision theory
steps.body: Chemical reactions can only happen when reactant particles collide with each other with enough energy. The minimum energy needed for a reaction is called the activation energy.

steps.title: Activation energy
steps.body: The minimum amount of energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur. Not all collisions lead to a reaction — only successful collisions with enough energy.

steps.title: Catalyst
steps.body: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. It works by lowering the activation energy, providing an alternative reaction pathway.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: There are three common methods for measuring the rate of a reaction: Method Measures Example Reaction Collecting gas volume over time Volume of gas produced Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ Mass lost over time Mass decreases as gas escapes CaCO₃ + HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ Colour change / disappearance Time for solution to become opaque Na₂S₂O₃ + HCl → sulfur precipitate Worked Example 3: Calculating rate from data In a reaction, 60 cm³ of hydrogen gas is produced in 120 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction. Rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 cm³/s

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Foundation State four factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction. | Foundation Explain, using collision theory, why increasing the concentration of a reactant increases the rate of reaction. | Higher A reaction produces 45 cm³ of gas in 90 seconds. Calculate the mean rate. Give the unit.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When explaining rate changes using collision theory, always mention both the frequency of collisions AND whether they have enough energy (activation energy) Temperature increases BOTH collision frequency AND collision energy — this is why it has the biggest effect on rate Concentration and surface area only increase collision frequency A catalyst does NOT change the amount of product formed — it only makes the reaction happen faster In rate calculations, rate = 1/time is only valid when comparing reactions that produce the same amount of product For graph questions, remember: gradient = rate, steeper = faster, plateau = reaction finished In required practical questions, always mention controlling variables for a fair test
